title: MotionJEPA: Preventing Temporal Feature Collapse by Capturing Visual Changes in Latent Space

paper.title: MotionJEPA: Preventing Temporal Feature Collapse by Capturing Visual Changes in Latent Space
paper.abstract:
Abstract Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) are a promising paradigm for learning task-agnostic latent world models without visual reconstruction.
However, standard JEPA training exhibits a strong inductive bias towards slow features, causing feature suppression and the collapse of latent representation.
While inverse dynamics provides temporal anti-collapse, it relies on action labels and offers little incentive to embed general, unlabeled dynamics.
We introduce D ifference I mage and S ingle image embedding Reg ularization (DISReg), a novel regularizer that builds on an inverse-dynamics-style module that predicts temporal difference image embeddings without any pixel reconstruction loss, encouraging balanced static and dynamic feature learning.
DISReg consists of a static term that shapes the distribution of the image embedding and encourages slow features, and a dynamic term, which, unlike direct regularization on the embedding, imposes no constraint on the image embedding’s shape or distribution and instead only incentivizes that dynamic features be present.
By integrating this regularizer into a standard JEPA, we establish our new architecture, MotionJEPA.
Latent probing demonstrates that MotionJEPA produces more complete representations than other methods, and our trajectory analysis shows it maintains geometrically simple latent embeddings with low curvature.
We further show that MotionJEPA improves downstream planning success under static-background distractors across four environments.
Code available: https://github.com/mkarmann/motion-jepa .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) [ 20 ] have emerged as a powerful paradigm for representation learning by predicting future states directly within an abstract embedding space. However, a fundamental question in training JEPA architectures lies in determining exactly which features the model should capture. Previous works such as [ 24 ] suggest encoding features that are either controlled by the agent or can affect the agent, ignoring uncontrollable background features. Yet the optimal feature hierarchy is inherently problem- and task-dependent. Short-time planning operates on a short timescale, predicting fast-changing dynamics, whereas long-time planning operates on larger timescales with slower-changing features [ 20 ] . Although the primary objective of JEPA frameworks is to learn task-agnostic world models, standard formulations exhibit a well-documented inductive bias toward encoding slow features [ 26 , 27 ] . In JEPA architectures, this trade-off is mainly controlled by the collapse prevention mechanism [ 26 ] . We illustrate this in Figure 1 , comparing SIGReg-based LeWorldModel [ 22 ] , inverse dynamics-based SMWM [ 18 ] , and our DISReg-based MotionJEPA. The D ifference I mage and S ingle image embedding Reg ularization (DISReg) is a novel regularizer that encourages a complementary and balanced embedding of both static and dynamic features. DISReg is made of two terms. The static term shapes the distribution of the single-image embedding, encouraging the slow features that standard JEPA training already favors. The dynamic term instead predicts the embedding of the temporal difference image from consecutive image embeddings. This dynamic term does not constrain the shape or distribution of the image embedding and only incentivizes that features that change between frames are present, which we show results in geometrically simple latent trajectories with low curvature in Table 2 . Our main contributions are as follows: • DISReg : A novel regularization term that incentivizes a balanced embedding of static and dynamic features by utilizing embeddings of the temporal difference images. • MotionJEPA : A novel JEPA framework that utilizes DISReg, demonstrating better downstream performance in the presence of static distractors and robustness to feature collapse. • A detailed collapse and latent trajectory analysis on a novel collection of three synthetic game environments (Pong, Dino, and Golf) with clearly separable, well-defined feature groups. • Downstream control evaluation on experiments demonstrating the strengths of MotionJEPA in the presence of static distractors. Figure 2 : MotionJEPA Overview . Our novel regularizer DISReg utilizes a temporal difference image embedding d t d_{t} as visually grounded collapse prevention for temporally changing features. The core JEPA encoder and predictor architecture concept is illustrated in blue, and our DISReg in green. The JEPA forward prediction loss, as well as DISReg losses are highlighted in red.

sections.heading: JEPA-style Latent World Models.
sections.text: The Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) is an architectural design that aims to learn latent representations without reconstructing the observation. As latent world models, these models learn to predict the dynamics of a system in latent space. The V-JEPA models [ 4 , 2 , 23 ] utilize a two-stage training paradigm by first pre-training on unlabeled video and then fine-tuning for the desired task. Recent work has further explored latent predictive models for control and planning, including LeWorldModel (LeWM) [ 22 ] , which learns action-conditioned dynamics directly in representation space, and DINO-WM [ 32 ] , which builds a world model on top of pretrained visual features for downstream planning tasks with Model Predictive Control (MPC). Temporal Difference in Vision (TDV) [ 9 ] does not require action labels and instead uses the pixel difference between consecutive frames to condition latent prediction and predict the corresponding change in representation space. Our work similarly exploits visually derived temporal change, but uses difference images as an auxiliary representation-learning objective to encourage the latent space to preserve changing scene information without requiring action labels.

sections.heading: Collapse Prevention in JEPA.
sections.text: Without a reconstruction loss, the main challenge of JEPAs is to avoid convergence to a trivial solution where all inputs map to a constant latent representation. Contrastive methods use negative samples to explicitly push embeddings apart [ 8 ] . Non-contrastive methods utilize stop-gradient teachers [ 1 , 4 , 2 , 23 , 9 ] . Other approaches avoid negative pairs entirely, such as VICReg, which prevents informational collapse by applying explicit variance, invariance, and covariance regularization directly to the embeddings [ 5 ] . More recent methods avoid computing heavy covariance matrices by shaping the latent space directly into an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Specifically, LeJEPA [ 3 ] introduces SIGReg as its sole collapse-prevention loss, using the Epps-Pulley test [ 10 ] rather than the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD) [ 6 ] to sketch the distribution. However, avoiding complete representational collapse does not ensure that the learned representation preserves all task-relevant factors of variation.

sections.heading: Feature Suppression and Slow-Feature Bias.
sections.text: Beyond complete collapse, self-supervised models may exhibit feature suppression , retaining only a subset of relevant information despite globally diverse representations [ 21 , 25 ] . In temporal predictive learning, this can appear as a preference for slowly varying features. While JEPA performs on par with or better than reconstruction-based methods in settings where noise changes every time step, JEPA-style models fail when fixed noise or features are present. Sobal et al. [26] show that JEPAs can encode fixed trajectory-specific distractors while neglecting faster foreground dynamics, a failure later reproduced across different noise timescales and predictive architectures [ 13 ] . Similar sensitivity to background changes has been observed in JEPA-based planning [ 28 ] , while recent theory further connects LeJEPA’s temporal alignment objective to Slow Feature Analysis [ 19 ] . LeNEPA [ 7 ] applies SIGReg along the time dimension instead of the batch dimension to encourage temporal diversity in the learned representation. Inverse dynamics provides another way to counteract this bias by forcing the representation to preserve information about action-relevant changes. Sensorimotor World Models (SMWM) [ 18 ] introduces an inverse model which predicts the action of two consecutive frames, given only the image embeddings. Experiments show that this additional module prevents collapse and enables the model to learn actual controllable degrees of freedom. Similarly, Delta-JEPA [ 31 ] also relies purely on the action prediction for collapse prevention, but provides the difference of two consecutive embeddings as input to the action decoder. A core limitation of inverse action prediction is that action labels are required. Additionally, these methods may be less suitable in scenarios where a given action causes a reaction in the observation with a time delay. These observations motivate our evaluation setting, where we introduce static background distractors into control environments to explicitly test whether the learned representation preserves changing, task-relevant scene information in the presence of strong slow features. Motivated by the same limitation, our method introduces a visually grounded temporal-difference objective that explicitly encourages the latent representation to preserve changing scene information without requiring action supervision.

sections.heading: Problem formulation.
sections.text: We are given an offline dataset of trajectories 𝒟 = { ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o T ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{T})\} with visual observations o t ∈ ℝ 3 × H obs × W obs o_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times H_{\text{obs}}\times W_{\text{obs}}} and continuous action labels a t ∈ ℝ D a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{a}} . The trajectories are not required to follow a task-specific policy and can be collected from any unknown or arbitrary behavior policy. The goal is to train a JEPA-style latent world model consisting of an encoder Enc θ : ℝ 3 × H obs × W obs → ℝ D z \text{Enc}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3\times H_{\text{obs}}\times W_{\text{obs}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}} that maps individual observations o t o_{t} to a latent state z t ∈ ℝ D z z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}} , and a forward predictor Pred ϕ \text{Pred}_{\phi} that estimates the deterministic state transition z ^ t + 1 = Pred ϕ ( z t − H + 1 : t , a t − H + 1 : t ) \hat{z}_{t+1}=\text{Pred}_{\phi}(z_{t-H+1:t},a_{t-H+1:t}) where H H is the size of the history context window. In the JEPA setting, this training process does not involve any reconstruction loss on the visual observations o t o_{t} , resulting in the primary challenge of preventing z t z_{t} from collapsing to trivial solutions [ 20 ] .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: The experiments are organized into two main sections. Sec. 4.1 investigates collapse scenarios on game environments with slow and static features by probing the latent embedding z z and further analyzing its path straightness. Sec. 4.2 demonstrates our method’s performance on downstream tasks with static distractors. Throughout all experiments, we use the same set of hyperparameters for MotionJEPA’s DISReg: λ z = 0.25 \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}=0.25 , λ pred = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{pred}}=0.5 , and λ d = 2 \lambda_{\mathrm{d}}=2 .

sections.heading: Baselines.
sections.text: We compare our method with previous end-to-end JEPA-style latent world models, namely LeWM [ 22 ] and SMWM [ 18 ] with default SIGReg weight of 0.09 0.09 for LeWM and inverse prediction weight of 1.0 1.0 for SMWM. We additionally provide altered versions of LeWM with common practice modifications used in the literature to improve robustness against feature collapse. LeWM-Time applies SIGReg along the time dimension [ 7 ] , LeWM-Flat applies SIGReg along the flattened batch and time dimension, and LeWM-Detached adds a StopGradient operator in the JEPA predictor loss target embedding MSE ​ ( StopGradient ​ ( z t + 1 ) , z ^ t + 1 ) \text{MSE}(\text{StopGradient}(z_{t+1}),\hat{z}_{t+1}) [ 12 , 1 , 4 ] . Besides these baselines, we also include ForwardOnly , which has only the forward prediction loss and no anti-collapse mechanism, and Random , with fixed, randomly initialized weights, showing what information is present in the latent at initialization that might be suppressed during training. Finally, we also perform a hyperparameter search for each baseline environment combination to demonstrate that the collapse is not an issue of hyperparameter selection but a fundamental limitation of JEPA anti-collapse mechanisms [ 26 ] . We mark such models with a star * throughout this work.

sections.heading: Environments.
sections.text: We designed three fully synthetic, deterministic game environments with clearly separable feature groups. Samples for each environment are generated on the fly during training and evaluation to prevent overfitting 1 1 1 Sampling is seeded to ensure that all methods observe identical training and evaluation sequences for a given seed. . Initial states and actions are sampled randomly for each episode to minimize correlations between features. This reduces the risk of shortcut learning [ 11 ] ; for example, in Pong, a probe estimating the bat’s position solely from the ball’s location would falsely suggest that bat information is encoded when it is not. We propose three environments of increasing dynamical complexity: Pong , where the agent controls both bats to hit the ball; Dino , a 2D side-scroller where an agent must jump over a cactus; and Golf , in which the player navigates a ball toward a hole while avoiding moving obstacles. We design the true state dimension of each environment (excluding velocities: Pong: 6, Dino: 8, Golf: 6) to be significantly lower than the latent embedding dimension D z D_{z} of 192 192 to ensure that the latent dimensionality is not a bottleneck that artificially induces collapse. Further implementation details for each environment are provided in Sec. 7 .

sections.heading: Evaluation Setup.
sections.text: We follow [ 26 ] and analyze the collapse of features by probing the learned image embedding z z . To keep the comparison fair, all methods use the same image encoder, latent forward predictor, training schedule, and optimizer from [ 22 ] . After training from scratch on 10M randomly sampled episodes, we freeze the base model, train probes on 1M training samples, and evaluate those probes on 10k episodes. For the collapse analysis, we choose higher-capacity MLP probes with residual connections instead of linear probe, as we are not interested in the linear separability or ease of accessibility of features, but rather in measuring the general presence or suppression of information in the latent embedding z z . For example, a world model which uses a non-linear, highly correlated representation in z z might still be functional, yet linear probes might fail to decode that information. We report Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) for each probe. An NMSE of 1.0 1.0 corresponds to predicting the evaluation target mean, indicating a complete failure to extract useful information from z z . We train and evaluate each method-environment pair for three seeds and report the average results. We provide more details about the training and evaluation process in Sec. 7 . sections.heading: Probing Results.
sections.text: Tab. 1 shows the MLP probing results on Pong, Dino, and Golf for both the encoder embeddings z z as well as predicted rollouts z ^ \hat{z} . The goal is to obtain the lowest average loss across all categories for each environment, indicating stable and balanced learning of all features 2 2 2 The average column presents a weighted mean, where each feature group’s weight corresponds to its dimensionality. . Looking at the results of probing the image embedding z z , as expected, the control method ForwardOnly collapsed on all three tasks, resulting in an NMSE greater than or about 1.0 1.0 for all features except the sky color of Dino, with 0.511 0.511 , which is arguably the easiest feature of these environments. Switching to the Random model, we observe that even though the weights are random, the probes are still able to extract a significant amount of information, with an NMSE average of 0.116 0.116 for Pong and even 0.004 0.004 for the sky in the Dino environment. This shows that even though the feature information is accessible at the start of training, models actively suppress it during training. Using default training parameters for LeWM results in clear collapses across all three environments, focusing only on slow or static features such as the score in Pong. While the hyperparameter-optimized version LeWM* improves the average probing loss on a simple task such as Pong from 0.658 0.658 to 0.061 0.061 , in the presence of more dynamic features, as in Dino and Golf, such hyperparameter optimization does not significantly improve results (see grid search in the appendix in Fig. 7 ), highlighting a core limitation of not regularizing along the time dimension. Both the LeWM-Flat* and LeWM-Time* variants add distribution constraints on the time dimension. LeWM-Time is the only model variant besides ours that successfully encodes the cactus in Dino, yet completely fails in the presence of more complex moving features in Golf. SMWM uses an inverse dynamics module that predicts the action of two consecutive states. It performs well on states which are directly impacted by actions but collapses on other task-relevant information. Our method achieves the lowest average feature probing loss across all three environments for both image embedding and rollout prediction while using the same set of hyperparameters across all three environments. MotionJEPA is also the only method that achieves a balanced probing loss below 0.1 0.1 on all categories, indicating robustness against feature collapse. Especially for the bar obstacle category of Golf, where MotionJEPA obtains 0.095 0.095 while all other methods suppress this category with losses higher than 0.3 0.3 . We also provide results with linear probes in Tab. 5 of the appendix, in which our model also achieves the lowest average probing loss across all environments.

sections.heading: When does collapse happen?
sections.text: In Fig. 3 we show the training loss curves with additional online MLP probes for the Dino environment. The probes are trained on the z z embedding with a stop-gradient operator to prevent information leaking to the encoder. The static sky and slow-changing hearts are the easiest features, quickly saturating at about 10k steps to 0.01 0.01 NMSE. We also observe that the random weights model is encoding these features as well. For LeWM, in which SIGReg is regularizing the distribution along the batch dimension, the slow features of the sky, hearts, and clouds suppress the embedding of the cactus and dinosaur. This is especially visible for the dinosaur, as the probing loss first decreases to approximately 0.1 0.1 at 5k iterations and then increases back to 1.0 1.0 at 20k iterations, from which it is not able to recover. LeWM-Flat, which enforces a distribution across both batch and time dimensions, seeks variance along the time dimension of the embedding as well and therefore quickly picks up the dinosaur. This is probably because its limited movement of jumping is very simple, but provides consistent temporal change. Crucially, the collapse is not visible in the training loss (see first column), demonstrating that monitoring loss alone is insufficient to diagnose collapse without explicit latent probing or downstream evaluation.

sections.heading: Latent Path Straightness.
sections.text: The temporal straightening hypothesis [ 14 ] states that useful representations turn curved input dynamics into near-straight latent paths. It has proven informative in practice, as a signal for identifying AI-generated video [ 15 ] , for judging physical plausibility [ 16 ] , and as a planning objective [ 29 ] . We show empirical results of the latent path straightness in Tab. 2 . SMWM achieves the straightest latent trajectories close to the ideal straight-line value of 1.0 1.0 in both Pong and Golf, as it has no distribution regularization on z z . Introducing distribution regularization along the time axis, such as in variants LeWM-Time* and LeWM-Flat* causes the opposite effect, significantly increasing the latent embedding curvature to above 20 20 for both Pong and Golf. As our method is architecturally closer to SMWM’s IDM module, we observe straighter paths than all distribution regularization methods on Pong and Golf. This can also be observed in Fig. 4 , where we show example latent trajectories of each feature of the golf environment. Our method produces nearly straight latent embeddings for ball position and single-loop embeddings for the circular cross and bar obstacles 3 3 3 The bar obstacles reappear on the opposite side if exiting the image and therefore result in a looped trajectory. . LeWM collapses all obstacles into almost a single point while showing high-curvature embeddings in the distracting wood background. While the representations of the LeWM-Flat variant do not collapse into a single point, the embedding has more curvature and entanglement, making it difficult to separate and predict individual features. sections.heading: 4.2 Downstream Tasks
sections.text: As in LeWorldModel [ 22 ] , probing is intended primarily as an analysis of representation content rather than to substitute for closed-loop control evaluation. We therefore take the experimental setup of LeWM [ 22 ] and evaluate the model’s success rate in the presence of slow features.

sections.heading: Environments.
sections.text: All four environments originally contain no static or slow visual features. To introduce a static-background distractor, we replace the original background with a wood-texture image, mimicking games played on a wooden table. For each rollout, a different crop of the texture image is sampled and kept fixed throughout the rollout. For PushT and TwoRoom, the original white background pixels are directly replaced with the wood texture. For Reacher and OG-Cube, we first estimate a static-background mask using the pixel-wise median over the training dataset and replace the corresponding regions with the texture. Example observations from all four environments are shown in Fig. 5 . All models are trained for 10 epochs with a batch size of 64 using AdamW, with a learning rate of 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} and weight decay of 10 − 3 10^{-3} .

sections.heading: Evaluation and Results.
sections.text: For evaluation, we use CEM-based planning following the protocol of the original LeWorldModel paper [ 22 ] . For IDM, we use our own implementation of inverse-dynamics supervision, predicting the raw action from Δ ​ z t = z t + 1 − z t \Delta z_{t}=z_{t+1}-z_{t} with a three-layer MLP. This follows the Δ ​ z \Delta z input formulation of DeltaJEPA [ 31 ] , while SMWM [ 18 ] similarly employs inverse-dynamics supervision with a different latent input parameterization. As an additional baseline, we evaluate LeWM-Flat, which applies SigReg after flattening the batch and temporal dimensions. Initial states are randomly sampled from the test split, and we evaluate planning horizons of 25 and 50 steps. For the 25-step setting, we follow the CEM planning configuration of [ 22 ] , using 300 candidate sequences, 30 elites, and the same environment-specific optimization budget. With a frame skip of 5, CEM plans five model steps ahead, corresponding to 25 environment steps. For the 50-step setting, we first plan and execute a 25-step trajectory, then replan from the resulting state for the remaining 25 steps using the same CEM configuration. The results are summarized in Table 3 . Overall, the original LeWM baseline degrades substantially in the presence of the static-background distractor, particularly on PushT and Reacher, while LeWM-Flat provides a stronger baseline but still remains clearly below IDM and our method in mean performance. IDM improves robustness across the four environments, while our standalone method achieves stronger overall mean performance, with particularly large gains on Cube and Reacher under the longer 50-step planning horizon. Combining our objective with IDM yields the best overall results, further indicating that the two training signals are complementary. On TwoRoom, both approaches achieve near-saturated performance, whereas the original LeWM baseline remains considerably lower. We further probe task-relevant states from the frozen representations on the four LeWorldModel benchmarks with static wood-texture distractors. Our method substantially improves state recoverability over LeWorldModel, consistent with its stronger downstream planning performance. sections.heading: Ablation Studies.
sections.text: For the four LeWM benchmark tasks, our method builds on LeWM and introduces an additional prediction objective using temporal difference images. As shown in Table 3 , removing the regularization on the original latent representation ( λ z = 0 \lambda_{z}=0 ) degrades performance, indicating that preserving global state information remains important alongside change-aware supervision. We further apply the same difference-image objective to the IDM-based LeWM variant and observe consistent improvements in 25-step planning, showing that the proposed objective is complementary to inverse-dynamics supervision and can serve as a useful add-on to existing world-model training.

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: DISReg introduces two additional modules, DiffEnc α \text{DiffEnc}_{\alpha} and DiffPred β \text{DiffPred}_{\beta} , both increasing the parameter count and compute cost relative to a plain JEPA baseline. However, the training loss curves in Fig. 3 show that collapse is not resolved simply by training longer or with more capacity. The baselines plateau in NMSE despite continued training, indicating that feature suppression is not an issue of compute budget. Furthermore, the modules introduced by DISReg are only relevant during training and are discarded afterward, adding no computational overhead during inference.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced DISReg, a regularizer that encourages JEPA world models to encode dynamic features by predicting an embedding of the temporal difference image, without action labels or pixel reconstruction. Integrated in MotionJEPA, our model captures both static and dynamic features more completely than prior methods, with straighter, less entangled latent trajectories, using one fixed hyperparameter set throughout. This translates to improved downstream planning under static-background distractors. Overall, encouraging dynamics through prediction rather than direct latent constraints offers a simple, effective route to collapse-resistant JEPA world models.

sections.heading: Encoder and Predictor Architecture.
sections.text: We use the same encoder and predictor architectures as [ 22 ] . The encoder is a ViT-Tiny Vision Transformer with a patch size of 14 × 14 14\times 14 pixels. As in [ 22 ] , the D z = 192 D_{z}=192 dimensional embedding vector is obtained from the [CLS] token of the final layer, followed by a 1-layer MLP with Batch Normalization [ 17 ] . The predictor is a six-layer causal transformer with 16 attention heads and learned positional embeddings [ 22 ] .

sections.heading: DISReg Components.
sections.text: We use the same architecture for the DiffEnc α \text{DiffEnc}_{\alpha} as for Enc θ \text{Enc}_{\theta} . The difference predictor DiffPred β \text{DiffPred}_{\beta} is a three-layer MLP with hidden layers of size 512 that uses LayerNorm and GELU after all but the final linear layer. The input is a concatenated vector of the two consecutive embeddings z t z_{t} and z t + 1 z_{t+1} .

sections.heading: Residual MLP Probe.
sections.text: The residual MLP probe has the highest capacity and is intended to check the general presence of information, not ease of accessibility. It is an MLP of depth 6 and width 128 with residual connections between every second layer and pre-activation batch normalization.

sections.heading: MLP Probe.
sections.text: We train a two-layer MLP on top of the frozen latent representation to measure non-linear accessibility of the states, comprising a linear layer with 512 hidden units, a GELU activation, and a final linear output layer. Angular targets are represented by their sine and cosine values and trained with MSE; angular error is computed after decoding the predicted angle.

sections.heading: Linear Probe.
sections.text: We train a single affine linear layer, including a bias term, on top of the frozen latent representation. No hidden layers, normalization, or activation functions are used. For LeWM benchmark problems, angular targets are represented by their sine and cosine values and trained with MSE; angular error is computed after decoding the predicted angle.

sections.heading: 7.2 Game Environments
sections.text: For all games, the states and actions are normalized to the range [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Initial states for the first frame and actions are sampled independently from a uniform distribution. These states are then simulated deterministically with the given actions to generate a total of 4 states and corresponding frames. Sample episodes of each dataset are shown in Fig. 6 .

sections.heading: 7.2.1 Pong
sections.text: State Variables : left bat position, right bat position, ball x-position, ball y-position, ball x-velocity, ball y-velocity, score left player, score right player. Actions : left bat velocity, right bat velocity. The positions of the ball and the players’ bats are also uniformly initialized. If a player hits the ball, the ball’s trajectory changes towards the opponent. The change in angle is dependent on the bat’s position, and the horizontal velocity accelerates with each hit up to a maximum velocity. If one player scores a goal, the score of the respective player increases by one, and the ball is reset to the center, moving towards the player who was scored against. The task requires the model to estimate the ball’s velocity in order to predict the ball’s next position.

sections.heading: 7.2.2 Dino
sections.text: State Variables : dinosaur y-position, dinosaur y-velocity, cactus x-position, cactus x-velocity, normalized number of hearts, sky color, clouds height, cloud 0 scroll, cloud 1 scroll, cloud 2 scroll. Actions : jump. A side scroller in which the goal is to time the dinosaur’s jumps to avoid upcoming cacti. Clouds each move with an individual fixed velocity for each episode. If the dinosaur collides with one of the cacti, the number of hearts is reduced by 1 (corresponding to a change of 0.1 0.1 in the normalized state vector). Once all lives are depleted, the game freezes for all remaining frames.

sections.heading: 7.2.3 Golf
sections.text: State Variables : ball x-position, ball y-position, cross angle, cross angular velocity, blue bar 1 x-scroll, blue bar 1 scroll x-velocity, blue bar 2 x-scroll, blue bar 2 x-scroll velocity, green bar y-scroll, green bar y-scroll velocity. Actions : ball x-velocity, ball y-velocity. In this game, the player navigates a ball through a 2D course of moving obstacles. Each obstacle is initialized at a random position, together with a random velocity that is fixed for each episode. The bars, when exiting the screen on one side, reappear on the other side of the screen. Colliding with obstacles stops the game, freezing it for the remaining frames and ignoring all action inputs. As the red cross is symmetric to one quarter of a full rotation, we normalize the cross angle to a range of 0 0 to 90 90 degrees.

sections.heading: 7.3 Details for Training on Game Environments
sections.text: Training and probe fitting use mixed-precision bfloat16 automatic mixed precision and torch.compile .

sections.heading: Pre-training on Game Environments.
sections.text: Experiments on the four game environments are conducted at a resolution of 112 × 112 112\times 112 pixels with no skip frames (i.e., simple next-frame prediction). We train the models using a history size of three on 10 million four-frame episodes with a batch size of 128, resulting in approximately 78k training steps. We use the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . For the learning rate, we employ a linear-warmup cosine-annealing schedule, matching the LeWM [ 22 ] defaults: the learning rate rises linearly from 0 0 to 5 × 10 − 5 5\times 10^{-5} over the first 1 % 1\% of training (781 steps), then decays to zero following a cosine schedule over the remaining steps. This schedule is stepped after every optimizer update.

sections.heading: Fitting Probes on Game Environment Models.
sections.text: After pre-training, we load and freeze the weights of the resulting encoder Enc θ \text{Enc}_{\theta} and predictor Pred ϕ \text{Pred}_{\phi} . We generate 1 million eight-frame episodes and, for each episode, embed the first three frames into latent vectors z 1 : 3 z_{1:3} using the encoder Enc θ \text{Enc}_{\theta} . Next, we use the first three embeddings z 1 : 3 z_{1:3} as context and apply the predictor Pred ϕ \text{Pred}_{\phi} autoregressively with a sliding window of size three and conditioned on the episode’s ground-truth actions to generate a rollout of five predicted embeddings z ^ 4 : 8 \hat{z}_{4:8} . Either image embeddings z 1 : 3 z_{1:3} or predicted rollout embeddings z ^ 4 : 8 \hat{z}_{4:8} are then used as inputs for the Residual MLP or Linear Probes. This results in a total of four probes: a Linear Probe on image embeddings, a Linear Probe on rollout embeddings, a Residual MLP Probe on image embeddings, and a Residual MLP Probe on rollout embeddings. The training target for each probe is the state vector detailed in Sec. 7.2 . We use the AdamW optimizer with a weight decay of 10 − 3 10^{-3} , a fixed learning rate of 3 × 10 − 3 3\times 10^{-3} , and a batch size of 128 128 . We evaluate each probe’s performance on an additional 10k episodes.

sections.text: For experiments on PushT , Two-Room , OG-Cube , and Reacher , we build on top of the original implementation provided by [ 22 ] together with the provided expert rollouts for each task. We use a history size of three for all four tasks. As in [ 22 ] , during episode sampling, we apply a 5-frame skip and group the consecutive actions between sampled frames into a single action vector. sections.heading: 8 Hyperparameter Search
sections.text: For baselines trained on the game environments, we perform a grid search over full 10M episode runs. For SMWM [ 18 ] , we grid-search the action-prediction loss weight; for LeWM [ 22 ] , LeWM-Detached, LeWM-Time, and LeWM-Flat, we grid-search the SIGReg weight. The selected configuration is the final run with the lowest NMSE of an offline 5-step Residual MLP probe, averaged over all probing-table state groups. We use the probe of the predicted rollout z ^ \hat{z} instead of the direct image embedding z z , as we are interested in a world model that is able to predict future states accurately, not a pure image embedding. Results of the hyperparameter search and sensitivity are shown in Tab. 4 and Fig. 7 .

sections.heading: Analysis.
sections.text: The probing results reveal substantial differences in the task-relevant physical information retained by the learned representations under static background distractors. LeWM performs poorly across several dynamic state variables, particularly on PushT, TwoRoom, and Reacher. LeWM-Flat improves recoverability in several cases, suggesting that stronger regularization over flattened batch and temporal dimensions partially alleviates the problem, but a substantial gap remains to the dynamics-aware objectives. For example, on PushT the MLP agent-position error decreases from 121.17 121.17 for LeWM to 55.67 55.67 for LeWM-Flat, while our method reaches 8.60 8.60 . Our method substantially improves physical-state recoverability across the evaluated environments. The effect is especially pronounced on Reacher, where the linear probe obtains joint-angle errors of 0.0265 0.0265 and 0.1246 0.1246 ,rad and a fingertip-position error of 0.0241 0.0241 , compared with 1.468 1.468 , 1.378 1.378 ,rad, and 0.169 0.169 for LeWM. The strong linear performance indicates that the controllable robot state is not only retained but also organized in a readily accessible form. IDM shows complementary behavior, providing particularly strong translational probing on PushT and OG-Cube, while remaining substantially weaker than our method on Reacher joint and fingertip states. Combining our objective with IDM further improves several controllable variables, including TwoRoom agent position and Reacher joint and fingertip states. Overall, the results support the interpretation that static-background degradation is associated with the representation emphasizing highly predictable visual content at the expense of task-relevant dynamics. Stronger SigReg alone, as in LeWM-Flat, helps but does not fully resolve this issue, while our objective and IDM provide stronger supervision for preserving dynamic physical state. Their combination further improves recoverability for several variables, consistent with the complementary planning gains observed in the main experiments.

However, standard JEPA training exhibits a strong inductive bias towards slow features, causing feature suppression and the collapse of latent representation. While inverse dynamics provides temporal anti-collapse, it relies on action labels and offers little incentive to embed general, unlabeled dynamics. We introduce D ifference I mage and S ingle image embedding Reg ularization (DISReg), a novel regularizer that builds on an inverse-dynamics-style module that predicts temporal difference image embeddings without any pixel reconstruction loss, encouraging balanced static and dynamic feature learning. DISReg consists of a static term that shapes the distribution of the image embedding and encourages slow features, and a dynamic term, which, unlike direct regularization on the embedding, imposes no constraint on the image embedding’s shape or distribution and instead only incentivizes that dynamic features be present. By integrating this regularizer into a standard JEPA, we establish our new architecture, MotionJEPA. Latent probing demonstrates that MotionJEPA produces more complete representations than other methods, and our trajectory analysis shows it maintains geometrically simple latent embeddings with low curvature. We further show that MotionJEPA improves downstream planning success under static-background distractors across four environments. Code available: https://github.com/mkarmann/motion-jepa . Figure 1 : Feature Suppression . We compare three JEPA variants that differ in collapse-prevention mechanisms: LeWM [ 22 ] (SIGReg), SMWM [ 18 ] (Inverse Dynamics Module, IDM), and our MotionJEPA, which uses DISReg. The Pong environment contains three features: a fast-moving ball, two bats, and a slow-changing scoreboard. When trained from scratch, visual probes of the image embeddings show that SIGReg encodes the slowly changing scoreboard and bats but suppresses the ball. IDM encodes only the action-controlled bats. DISReg preserves all three. 1 Introduction Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) [ 20 ] have emerged as a powerful paradigm for representation learning by predicting future states directly within an abstract embedding space. However, a fundamental question in training JEPA architectures lies in determining exactly which features the model should capture. Previous works such as [ 24 ] suggest encoding features that are either controlled by the agent or can affect the agent, ignoring uncontrollable background features. Yet the optimal feature hierarchy is inherently problem- and task-dependent. Short-time planning operates on a short timescale, predicting fast-changing dynamics, whereas long-time planning operates on larger timescales with slower-changing features [ 20 ] . Although the primary objective of JEPA frameworks is to learn task-agnostic world models, standard formulations exhibit a well-documented inductive bias toward encoding slow features [ 26 , 27 ] . In JEPA architectures, this trade-off is mainly controlled by the collapse prevention mechanism [ 26 ] . We illustrate this in Figure 1 , comparing SIGReg-based LeWorldModel [ 22 ] , inverse dynamics-based SMWM [ 18 ] , and our DISReg-based MotionJEPA. The D ifference I mage and S ingle image embedding Reg ularization (DISReg) is a novel regularizer that encourages a complementary and balanced embedding of both static and dynamic features. DISReg is made of two terms. The static term shapes the distribution of the single-image embedding, encouraging the slow features that standard JEPA training already favors. The dynamic term instead predicts the embedding of the temporal difference image from consecutive image embeddings. This dynamic term does not constrain the shape or distribution of the image embedding and only incentivizes that features that change between frames are present, which we show results in geometrically simple latent trajectories with low curvature in Table 2 . Our main contributions are as follows: • DISReg : A novel regularization term that incentivizes a balanced embedding of static and dynamic features by utilizing embeddings of the temporal difference images. • MotionJEPA : A novel JEPA framework that utilizes DISReg, demonstrating better downstream performance in the presence of static distractors and robustness to feature collapse. • A detailed collapse and latent trajectory analysis on a novel collection of three synthetic game environments (Pong, Dino, and Golf) with clearly separable, well-defined feature groups. • Downstream control evaluation on experiments demonstrating the strengths of MotionJEPA in the presence of static distractors. Figure 2 : MotionJEPA Overview . Our novel regularizer DISReg utilizes a temporal difference image embedding d t d_{t} as visually grounded collapse prevention for temporally changing features. The core JEPA encoder and predictor architecture concept is illustrated in blue, and our DISReg in green. The JEPA forward prediction loss, as well as DISReg losses are highlighted in red. 2 Related Work JEPA-style Latent World Models. The Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) is an architectural design that aims to learn latent representations without reconstructing the observation. As latent world models, these models learn to predict the dynamics of a system in latent space. The V-JEPA models [ 4 , 2 , 23 ] utilize a two-stage training paradigm by first pre-training on unlabeled video and then fine-tuning for the desired task. Recent work has further explored latent predictive models for control and planning, including LeWorldModel (LeWM) [ 22 ] , which learns action-conditioned dynamics directly in representation space, and DINO-WM [ 32 ] , which builds a world model on top of pretrained visual features for downstream planning tasks with Model Predictive Control (MPC). Temporal Difference in Vision (TDV) [ 9 ] does not require action labels and instead uses the pixel difference between consecutive frames to condition latent prediction and predict the corresponding change in representation space. Our work similarly exploits visually derived temporal change, but uses difference images as an auxiliary representation-learning objective to encourage the latent space to preserve changing scene information without requiring action labels. Collapse Prevention in JEPA. Without a reconstruction loss, the main challenge of JEPAs is to avoid convergence to a trivial solution where all inputs map to a constant latent representation. Contrastive methods use negative samples to explicitly push embeddings apart [ 8 ] . Non-contrastive methods utilize stop-gradient teachers [ 1 , 4 , 2 , 23 , 9 ] . Other approaches avoid negative pairs entirely, such as VICReg, which prevents informational collapse by applying explicit variance, invariance, and covariance regularization directly to the embeddings [ 5 ] . More recent methods avoid computing heavy covariance matrices by shaping the latent space directly into an isotropic Gaussian distribution. Specifically, LeJEPA [ 3 ] introduces SIGReg as its sole collapse-prevention loss, using the Epps-Pulley test [ 10 ] rather than the Sliced Wasserstein Distance (SWD) [ 6 ] to sketch the distribution. However, avoiding complete representational collapse does not ensure that the learned representation preserves all task-relevant factors of variation. Feature Suppression and Slow-Feature Bias. Beyond complete collapse, self-supervised models may exhibit feature suppression , retaining only a subset of relevant information despite globally diverse representations [ 21 , 25 ] . In temporal predictive learning, this can appear as a preference for slowly varying features. While JEPA performs on par with or better than reconstruction-based methods in settings where noise changes every time step, JEPA-style models fail when fixed noise or features are present. Sobal et al. [26] show that JEPAs can encode fixed trajectory-specific distractors while neglecting faster foreground dynamics, a failure later reproduced across different noise timescales and predictive architectures [ 13 ] . Similar sensitivity to background changes has been observed in JEPA-based planning [ 28 ] , while recent theory further connects LeJEPA’s temporal alignment objective to Slow Feature Analysis [ 19 ] . LeNEPA [ 7 ] applies SIGReg along the time dimension instead of the batch dimension to encourage temporal diversity in the learned representation. Inverse dynamics provides another way to counteract this bias by forcing the representation to preserve information about action-relevant changes. Sensorimotor World Models (SMWM) [ 18 ] introduces an inverse model which predicts the action of two consecutive frames, given only the image embeddings. Experiments show that this additional module prevents collapse and enables the model to learn actual controllable degrees of freedom. Similarly, Delta-JEPA [ 31 ] also relies purely on the action prediction for collapse prevention, but provides the difference of two consecutive embeddings as input to the action decoder. A core limitation of inverse action prediction is that action labels are required. Additionally, these methods may be less suitable in scenarios where a given action causes a reaction in the observation with a time delay. These observations motivate our evaluation setting, where we introduce static background distractors into control environments to explicitly test whether the learned representation preserves changing, task-relevant scene information in the presence of strong slow features. Motivated by the same limitation, our method introduces a visually grounded temporal-difference objective that explicitly encourages the latent representation to preserve changing scene information without requiring action supervision. 3 Method Problem formulation. We are given an offline dataset of trajectories 𝒟 = { ( o 1 , a 1 , … , o T ) } \mathcal{D}=\{(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{T})\} with visual observations o t ∈ ℝ 3 × H obs × W obs o_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{3\times H_{\text{obs}}\times W_{\text{obs}}} and continuous action labels a t ∈ ℝ D a a_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{a}} . The trajectories are not required to follow a task-specific policy and can be collected from any unknown or arbitrary behavior policy. The goal is to train a JEPA-style latent world model consisting of an encoder Enc θ : ℝ 3 × H obs × W obs → ℝ D z \text{Enc}_{\theta}:\mathbb{R}^{3\times H_{\text{obs}}\times W_{\text{obs}}}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}} that maps individual observations o t o_{t} to a latent state z t ∈ ℝ D z z_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{D_{z}} , and a forward predictor Pred ϕ \text{Pred}_{\phi} that estimates the deterministic state transition z ^ t + 1 = Pred ϕ ( z t − H + 1 : t , a t − H + 1 : t ) \hat{z}_{t+1}=\text{Pred}_{\phi}(z_{t-H+1:t},a_{t-H+1:t}) where H H is the size of the history context window. In the JEPA setting, this training process does not involve any reconstruction loss on the visual observations o t o_{t} , resulting in the primary challenge of preventing z t z_{t} from collapsing to trivial solutions [ 20 ] . Collapse prevention with DISReg. Sec. 4.1 investigates collapse scenarios on game environments with slow and static features by probing the latent embedding z z and further analyzing its path straightness. Sec. 4.2 demonstrates our method’s performance on downstream tasks with static distractors. Throughout all experiments, we use the same set of hyperparameters for MotionJEPA’s DISReg: λ z = 0.25 \lambda_{\mathrm{z}}=0.25 , λ pred = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{pred}}=0.5 , and λ d = 2 \lambda_{\mathrm{d}}=2 . Baselines. We compare our method with previous end-to-end JEPA-style latent world models, namely LeWM [ 22 ] and SMWM [ 18 ] with default SIGReg weight of 0.09 0.09 for LeWM and inverse prediction weight of 1.0 1.0 for SMWM. We additionally provide altered versions of LeWM with common practice modifications used in the literature to improve robustness against feature collapse. LeWM-Time applies SIGReg along the time dimension [ 7 ] , LeWM-Flat applies SIGReg along the flattened batch and time dimension, and LeWM-Detached adds a StopGradient operator in the JEPA predictor loss target embedding MSE ​ ( StopGradient ​ ( z t + 1 ) , z ^ t + 1 ) \text{MSE}(\text{StopGradient}(z_{t+1}),\hat{z}_{t+1}) [ 12 , 1 , 4 ] . Besides these baselines, we also include ForwardOnly , which has only the forward prediction loss and no anti-collapse mechanism, and Random , with fixed, randomly initialized weights, showing what information is present in the latent at initialization that might be suppressed during training. Finally, we also perform a hyperparameter search for each baseline environment combination to demonstrate that the collapse is not an issue of hyperparameter selection but a fundamental limitation of JEPA anti-collapse mechanisms [ 26 ] . We mark such models with a star * throughout this work. 4.1 Collapse and Latent Embedding Analysis Environments. We designed three fully synthetic, deterministic game environments with clearly separable feature groups. Samples for each environment are generated on the fly during training and evaluation to prevent overfitting 1 1 1 Sampling is seeded to ensure that all methods observe identical training and evaluation sequences for a given seed. . Initial states and actions are sampled randomly for each episode to minimize correlations between features. This reduces the risk of shortcut learning [ 11 ] ; for example, in Pong, a probe estimating the bat’s position solely from the ball’s location would falsely suggest that bat information is encoded when it is not. We propose three environments of increasing dynamical complexity: Pong , where the agent controls both bats to hit the ball; Dino , a 2D side-scroller where an agent must jump over a cactus; and Golf , in which the player navigates a ball toward a hole while avoiding moving obstacles. We design the true state dimension of each environment (excluding velocities: Pong: 6, Dino: 8, Golf: 6) to be significantly lower than the latent embedding dimension D z D_{z} of 192 192 to ensure that the latent dimensionality is not a bottleneck that artificially induces collapse. Further implementation details for each environment are provided in Sec. 7 . Evaluation Setup. We follow [ 26 ] and analyze the collapse of features by probing the learned image embedding z z . To keep the comparison fair, all methods use the same image encoder, latent forward predictor, training schedule, and optimizer from [ 22 ] . After training from scratch on 10M randomly sampled episodes, we freeze the base model, train probes on 1M training samples, and evaluate those probes on 10k episodes. For the collapse analysis, we choose higher-capacity MLP probes with residual connections instead of linear probe, as we are not interested in the linear separability or ease of accessibility of features, but rather in measuring the general presence or suppression of information in the latent embedding z z . For example, a world model which uses a non-linear, highly correlated representation in z z might still be functional, yet linear probes might fail to decode that information. We report Normalized Mean Squared Error (NMSE) for each probe. An NMSE of 1.0 1.0 corresponds to predicting the evaluation target mean, indicating a complete failure to extract useful information from z z . We train and evaluate each method-environment pair for three seeds and report the average results. We provide more details about the training and evaluation process in Sec. 7 . Looking at the results of probing the image embedding z z , as expected, the control method ForwardOnly collapsed on all three tasks, resulting in an NMSE greater than or about 1.0 1.0 for all features except the sky color of Dino, with 0.511 0.511 , which is arguably the easiest feature of these environments. Switching to the Random model, we observe that even though the weights are random, the probes are still able to extract a significant amount of information, with an NMSE average of 0.116 0.116 for Pong and even 0.004 0.004 for the sky in the Dino environment. This shows that even though the feature information is accessible at the start of training, models actively suppress it during training. Using default training parameters for LeWM results in clear collapses across all three environments, focusing only on slow or static features such as the score in Pong. While the hyperparameter-optimized version LeWM* improves the average probing loss on a simple task such as Pong from 0.658 0.658 to 0.061 0.061 , in the presence of more dynamic features, as in Dino and Golf, such hyperparameter optimization does not significantly improve results (see grid search in the appendix in Fig. 7 ), highlighting a core limitation of not regularizing along the time dimension. Both the LeWM-Flat* and LeWM-Time* variants add distribution constraints on the time dimension. LeWM-Time is the only model variant besides ours that successfully encodes the cactus in Dino, yet completely fails in the presence of more complex moving features in Golf. SMWM uses an inverse dynamics module that predicts the action of two consecutive states. It performs well on states which are directly impacted by actions but collapses on other task-relevant information. Our method achieves the lowest average feature probing loss across all three environments for both image embedding and rollout prediction while using the same set of hyperparameters across all three environments. MotionJEPA is also the only method that achieves a balanced probing loss below 0.1 0.1 on all categories, indicating robustness against feature collapse. Especially for the bar obstacle category of Golf, where MotionJEPA obtains 0.095 0.095 while all other methods suppress this category with losses higher than 0.3 0.3 . We also provide results with linear probes in Tab. 5 of the appendix, in which our model also achieves the lowest average probing loss across all environments. When does collapse happen? In Fig. 3 we show the training loss curves with additional online MLP probes for the Dino environment. The probes are trained on the z z embedding with a stop-gradient operator to prevent information leaking to the encoder. The static sky and slow-changing hearts are the easiest features, quickly saturating at about 10k steps to 0.01 0.01 NMSE. We also observe that the random weights model is encoding these features as well. For LeWM, in which SIGReg is regularizing the distribution along the batch dimension, the slow features of the sky, hearts, and clouds suppress the embedding of the cactus and dinosaur. This is especially visible for the dinosaur, as the probing loss first decreases to approximately 0.1 0.1 at 5k iterations and then increases back to 1.0 1.0 at 20k iterations, from which it is not able to recover. LeWM-Flat, which enforces a distribution across both batch and time dimensions, seeks variance along the time dimension of the embedding as well and therefore quickly picks up the dinosaur. This is probably because its limited movement of jumping is very simple, but provides consistent temporal change. Crucially, the collapse is not visible in the training loss (see first column), demonstrating that monitoring loss alone is insufficient to diagnose collapse without explicit latent probing or downstream evaluation. Latent Path Straightness. The temporal straightening hypothesis [ 14 ] states that useful representations turn curved input dynamics into near-straight latent paths. It has proven informative in practice, as a signal for identifying AI-generated video [ 15 ] , for judging physical plausibility [ 16 ] , and as a planning objective [ 29 ] . We show empirical results of the latent path straightness in Tab. 2 . SMWM achieves the straightest latent trajectories close to the ideal straight-line value of 1.0 1.0 in both Pong and Golf, as it has no distribution regularization on z z . Introducing distribution regularization along the time axis, such as in variants LeWM-Time* and LeWM-Flat* causes the opposite effect, significantly increasing the latent embedding curvature to above 20 20 for both Pong and Golf. As our method is architecturally closer to SMWM’s IDM module, we observe straighter paths than all distribution regularization methods on Pong and Golf.
